interviewQuestions.question: How would you use the Adapter pattern to integrate a third-party library with an incompatible interface?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the interface my code already depends on — say `Logger.log(message)` — and the interface the new library actually exposes, which won't match. Rather than rewriting either side, I'd write a small adapter class that implements `Logger` and internally calls the library's real method, translating arguments and, importantly, translating exceptions too so the library's own error types never leak past the adapter.

I'd walk through a concrete example: wrapping a payment SDK's `charge(amountCents, token)` behind my own `PaymentProcessor.charge(amount, card)` interface, so switching providers later means writing one new adapter, not touching business logic anywhere else.

**Testing:** whether you isolate an external dependency behind one seam instead of spreading its shape through your codebase.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Integrating an incompatible third-party library

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between Adapter and Decorator — both wrap an object, so how do you tell them apart in an interview?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd anchor on intent, since the mechanics (wrap one object, hold a reference to it) look almost identical. Adapter exists because two interfaces don't match — it translates method signatures so a client can use a class it wasn't written for, and it adds no new behavior. Decorator exists because you want to add responsibility to an object that already speaks the right interface — compression, encryption, logging — while keeping that interface unchanged.

A quick test I'd mention: if removing the wrapper would break compilation because the interfaces genuinely don't match, it's Adapter. If removing the wrapper still compiles and just drops a feature, it's Decorator.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish patterns by intent, not by their superficially similar wrap-and-delegate shape.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Adapter vs Decorator

interviewQuestions.question: When would you NOT reach for Adapter, even though the interfaces technically don't match?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd flag two cases. First, if I own both interfaces and they've simply drifted apart over time, I'd fix the interface directly rather than institutionalize the mismatch with a permanent adapter — that's paying interest on design debt forever instead of fixing the principal. Second, if the mismatch is so deep that adapting it needs dozens of special-case translation rules, that usually signals the two systems model the domain differently enough that a thin translation layer will be fragile; I'd consider a proper redesign or an anti-corruption layer with real domain logic instead of calling it "just an adapter."

**Testing:** whether you can recognize when a pattern is being used to avoid a harder, correct fix.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: When not to use Adapter
